title: Bioconductor All‑Community Handbook
text: Preface

title: Bioconductor All‑Community Handbook
text:
Welcome
Welcome to the Bioconductor All‑Community Handbook (BACH).
This handbook is a collaborative effort to capture and share knowledge about the Bioconductor community, its practices, and its resources. It is intended for anyone interested in contributing to or learning from the Bioconductor community, whether you are a seasoned contributor or a newcomer.
This book was initiated during a BioFAIR Collaboration Fest held at The Open University on 15-17 September 2026. It began as an effort to capture FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) practices not covered by existing Bioconductor materials, but discussions broadened its scope into a handbook bringing together key aspects of community practice in one place.
The structure of this handbook is inspired from The Turing Way, referring to it for more general guidance on open source software development, data science, and reproducible research. It is intended to unify this combined knowledge under one common roof while signposting to more specialised guidance maintained by Bioconductor and other communities.

title: Guide for Software
text:
This guide will cover practices and resources for the design, maintenance, and peer review of Bioconductor software.
Those practices and resources are currently described in the bookdown book Bioconductor Packages: Development, Maintenance, and Peer Review.

text:
This section will cover practices and resources for developing Bioconductor packages.

title: Guide for Communication
text:
This guide will provide practical advice for communicating within the Bioconductor community and with other communities.
It will define shared language, identify where to ask questions and share needs, and describe how users, developers, trainers, and maintainers can collaborate effectively within and beyond Bioconductor.

title: Community communication channels
text:
The bioc-devel mailing list
Bioconductor community members use several platforms for questions, discussion, and coordination. Choose the channel that best fits your needs.
Created in March 2004, the bioc-devel mailing list is for package development and Bioconductor infrastructure questions, particularly when input from developers or the core team may be needed.
New users can subscribe to the mailing list at https://stat.ethz.ch/mailman/listinfo/bioc-devel.

title: Community communication channels
text:
The Bioconductor support site
Launched in August 2014, the Bioconductor support site is the best place for questions about using Bioconductor packages. Its archived, searchable answers can help future users with the same issue.
The support site is available at https://support.bioconductor.org, where new users can freely create an account to post questions and answers.

title: Community communication channels
text:
The Bioconductor Zulip chat
Bioconductor uses Zulip, a freely accessible, open-source chat platform, for community discussion, brainstorming, coordination, introductions, announcements, mentoring, working groups, and event planning.
New users can sign up at https://chat.bioconductor.org/. See Using the Bioconductor Zulip chat for an introduction to channels, topics, and getting started.

title: Community communication channels
text:
Additional resources

Bioconductor Support and Community Forum
Bioconductor Posting Guide

title: Using the Bioconductor Zulip chat
text:
Understanding channels and topics
Bioconductor uses Zulip, a freely accessible, open-source chat platform, for community discussion, brainstorming, coordination, introductions, announcements, mentoring, working groups, and event planning.
New users can sign up at https://chat.bioconductor.org/. See Using the Bioconductor Zulip chat for an introduction to channels, topics, and getting started.
Zulip organises messages into channels and topics:
For example, a conversation in education-and-training might have the topic “Finding introductory RNA-seq materials”.

title: Using the Bioconductor Zulip chat
text:
A channel is a broad area of interest, such as education-and-training or events.
A topic is the subject of a conversation within that channel. Think of it like an email subject line.

title: Using the Bioconductor Zulip chat
text:
Starting or joining a conversation
To ask a new question or start a conversation, choose a relevant channel and give your topic a short, descriptive title, just as you would write a subject line for a new email.
To reply to a conversation you are reading, write in that conversation’s existing topic, just as you would reply to an email thread.
You don’t need to search through old topics or find a perfect match before asking a new question. If someone knows of a related discussion, they can point you to it.






TipNot sure where to post?



Try #general, or #no-stupid-questions for questions about Bioconductor, R, and the community.
You don’t need to find the perfect channel or topic title before posting. Other community members can help, and messages can be moved if needed.
For help troubleshooting a specific Bioconductor package, please use the support site.

title: Using the Bioconductor Zulip chat
text:
Finding channels and following discussions
New members are subscribed to four channels to get started:

general: Community discussions and updates.
random: Informal chat.
introductions: Introduce yourself and meet other members.
events: Workshops, talks, and conferences.

There are also channels for scientific interests, software development, training, regional communities, and specific projects.
Click Browse more channels at the bottom of your channel list to explore and subscribe. You’re welcome to join any public channel that interests you.
You don’t need to follow everything. Start with a few channels, read along if you prefer, and join conversations when you have a question or something to share.

title: Using the Bioconductor Zulip chat
section: A short tour and further help
text:
A short tour and further help
Watch the two-minute Zulip tour for a demonstration of channels, topics, navigation, and starting a conversation.
For more detailed instructions, see Zulip’s getting-started guide.






NoteOur move from Slack



The community previously used Slack for chat. We moved to Zulip on 2 June 2025 to ensure long-term access to discussions and better reflect the community’s open-source values.
Read more in Bioconductor is Moving from Slack to Zulip for Community Chat.

title: Communicating with package authors
text:
Choosing the appropriate communication channel
Bioconductor packages are developed and maintained by members of the scientific community. Much of this work is carried out on a voluntary basis, often alongside research, teaching, and other professional responsibilities.
Although package maintainers are expected to provide ongoing support, their time and availability may be limited. When seeking help, it is important to communicate respectfully, provide sufficient information, and use the appropriate communication channels.
The following channels are listed in their recommended order of preference, depending on the nature of your request.

title: Communicating with package authors
text:
1. Bioconductor Support Site
The Bioconductor Support Site is the preferred channel for most questions about using Bioconductor packages.
Use it when:

Asking how to use a package or a particular function.
Seeking clarification about package documentation or behaviour.
Encountering errors or unexpected results.
Requesting help with an analysis involving Bioconductor packages.

What to do:

Search the Support Site to check whether a similar question has already been answered.
Create a new post with a descriptive title explaining your question or problem.
Tag your post with the names of the relevant packages. This is particularly important because package tags automatically trigger email notifications to the corresponding maintainers. Package names must be spelled correctly, although capitalisation does not matter.
Provide a reproducible example whenever possible, including relevant code, error messages, and the output of sessionInfo().
Continue the conversation publicly by adding comments to the original post rather than switching to private communication.

Using the Support Site allows other community members to contribute answers and creates a searchable record that can help users facing similar problems.
For more information, consult the Bioconductor Posting Guide.


2. Package issue tracker
Many Bioconductor packages have a dedicated issue tracker, for instance hosted on the corresponding GitHub repository. This can be the most appropriate channel for reporting software defects or proposing improvements.
Use it when:

Reporting a reproducible software bug.
Requesting a new feature or enhancement.
Identifying a problem with the package documentation.
Proposing a specific change to the package implementation.

What to do:

Visit the package’s landing page on the Bioconductor website.
Look for a Bug Reports link, or inspect the BugReports field in the package’s DESCRIPTION file.
Check existing issues to avoid reporting something that is already known.
Open a new issue describing the problem or proposed improvement, following any contribution guidelines provided by the maintainers.
For bug reports, include a minimal reproducible example, relevant error messages, and information about your software environment.

Do not assume that every GitHub repository is actively monitored. Some contributed Bioconductor packages have no associated GitHub repository, or their repository may not be up to date.
Issue trackers should generally not be used for routine questions about how to use a package. Those questions are better suited to the Bioconductor Support Site.


3. Bioconductor developer mailing list
The Bioconductor developer mailing list (bioc-devel) is intended for discussions about package development and the broader Bioconductor software ecosystem.
Use it when:

Asking questions about developing or maintaining a Bioconductor package.
Discussing package development practices or Bioconductor infrastructure.
Seeking advice about changes that could affect multiple packages.
Discussing proposed improvements to the Bioconductor ecosystem.

What to do:

Check whether your question concerns package development rather than package usage.
Search previous discussions for relevant information.
Send a clearly formulated message to bioc-devel@r-project.org, including enough technical context for other developers to respond.
Keep the discussion on the mailing list so that other developers can benefit.

Messages from people who are not subscribed to the mailing list may require moderator approval.
The developer mailing list is not generally intended for routine package usage questions.


4. Bioconductor Zulip
The Bioconductor Zulip brings together users and developers in specialised channels for questions and collaboration, as described on the Bioconductor Support and Community Forum page. It can be a useful way to reach package authors who participate in a channel relevant to your topic.
Use it when:

A suitable public channel exists for the package, research area, or development topic you want to discuss.
Seeking informal discussion or exploring collaboration with package authors and other community members.
Continuing a relevant discussion already taking place on Zulip.

What to do:

Browse the available channels and read their descriptions to check whether your topic fits.
Search previous conversations before starting a new discussion.
Reply in an existing topic if it matches your question, or start a new topic with a descriptive title in the appropriate channel.
Include the package name, relevant context, and links to any related Support Site posts or issues.
Keep the conversation in the public channel so that other community members can contribute and benefit.

If no suitable channel exists, use one of the other communication channels described above. The Bioconductor Support Site remains the preferred place for routine package usage questions. Do not assume that every package author uses Zulip or monitors a particular channel, or expect an immediate response.






Important



Avoid unsolicited direct messages (DMs) for technical support. Like direct emails, DMs limit who can help and prevent the wider community from benefiting from the answer. The same considerations for private contact in the direct email section below apply to Zulip DMs: use them only when invited or when the matter genuinely requires private communication.




5. Direct email to package maintainers
Direct email should only be a last resort to reach the maintainer of a Bioconductor package.
The email address of the package maintainer can be found in the Maintainer: section of the package’s landing page on the Bioconductor website.
The Bioconductor Posting Guide explicitly recommends keeping conversations on the Support Site and avoiding direct email unless the other party indicates otherwise.
Direct email may nevertheless be appropriate when:

The maintainer has explicitly invited you to contact them by email.
The matter involves confidential or sensitive information that cannot reasonably be discussed publicly.
You wish to discuss a potential collaboration or another matter unrelated to routine technical support.
A specific situation requires private communication and no suitable public channel is available.

What to do:

Check whether the package documentation provides a preferred contact method.
If direct contact is appropriate, find the maintainer’s email address in the package’s DESCRIPTION file or Bioconductor landing page.
Write a concise message explaining the purpose of your contact.
Include relevant context and, where applicable, links to previous public discussions.
Respect the maintainer’s availability and avoid repeated follow-up messages over short periods.







Note



The presence of an email address in a package’s metadata does not imply that direct email is the preferred support channel. This address also serves an important administrative purpose, allowing the Bioconductor project to contact maintainers about their packages.

title: Communicating with package authors
text:
General recommendations
Regardless of the communication channel, following a few simple practices makes it easier for maintainers and other community members to help.

Consult existing resources first. Read the package documentation, vignettes, and relevant discussions before posting a new question.
Be specific. Explain what you are trying to achieve, what you have attempted, and what happened.
Make problems reproducible. Provide a minimal example, relevant outputs, and your R session information whenever possible.
Use public channels whenever appropriate. Public discussions make solutions discoverable and reduce repeated requests to maintainers.
Be respectful and patient. Package maintenance and community support frequently rely on voluntary contributions. Responses may take time, and immediate assistance cannot be guaranteed.
Follow the Bioconductor Code of Conduct. Keep interactions professional, constructive, and considerate of others.

Remember that package maintainers are responsible for maintaining their software, but they are not necessarily available to provide individual, on-demand support. Choosing the appropriate channel and asking well-structured questions helps sustain a welcoming and effective support community.

title: Communicating with package authors
text:
Further reading
This guidance is based on the following official Bioconductor resources:

Bioconductor Posting Guide — Recommendations for asking questions, communicating with maintainers, and participating in support discussions.
Bioconductor Support and Community Forum — Overview of available communication channels and their intended purposes.
Bioconductor Author / Maintainer Expectations — Responsibilities of package maintainers, including responding to user questions and monitoring support channels.

title: Communicating with other communities
text: This section will introduce communication practices, resources, and pathways for coordinating work and building effective relationships with other projects and communities.

title: Guide for FAIR Practices
text: As part of the Bioconductor community, we develop and maintain open-source software, data, and training resources. By applying the FAIR principles – Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable – this guide will cover practices and resources supporting users and developers in making those resources easier to discover, access, integrate, and reuse within and beyond the Bioconductor ecosystem. The following sections describe processes, resources, and checklists for producing FAIR Bioconductor tools, wrappers and workflows, including integrations with other software ecosystems.

title: Interoperable file types
text:
Saving Bioconductor objects for sharing
Bioconductor objects provide a shared structure for data and metadata within the project. However, preserving their rich metadata in file formats that remain usable over time and across programming languages can be challenging.
The workflow package savingBiocObjects offers guidance on saving and sharing Bioconductor objects, with examples covering common Bioconductor classes and standard file formats.

title: Interoperable file types
text:
Note



A Bioconductor workflow package primarily provides vignettes demonstrating an analysis or task, found in the Documentation section of its package webpage. At the time of writing, savingBiocObjects contains a single vignette: Saving Bioconductor objects.

title: Bioconductor in Galaxy
section: Galaxy file types for Bioconductor objects
text:
Galaxy file types for Bioconductor objects
How are R objects stored on disk in Galaxy? What are the preferred file types for interoperability with other programming languages and software ecosystems?
For example, this GitHub issue has been discussing insecure aspects of RData files. While those are the default file type for R objects, they are not interoperable with other programming languages and software ecosystems. Instead, the loom file format has gained popularity as a preferred file type for disk-based storage of R objects, and is interoperable with other programming languages and software ecosystems

title: Code of Conduct
text:
The Bioconductor Code of Conduct was initially adapted from the BioC 2020 Code of Conduct, which itself built on earlier conference-specific documents.
Changes to the Code of Conduct are versioned and tracked over time. Each translation is version-controlled and corresponds to a specific version of the reference U.S. English document.






NoteCode of Conduct translations



Existing translations of the Code of Conduct are currently being transferred into this repository. During this transition, readers are encouraged to consult the Bioconductor multilingual Code of Conduct site for potentially more up-to-date translations.

title: Code of Conduct (U.S. English)
text:
Version 1.5.0 (18th March, 2026)
The Bioconductor community values an open approach to science that promotes:
In line with these values, Bioconductor is dedicated to providing a welcoming, supportive, collegial experience free of harassment, intimidation, and bullying regardless of:
By participating in this community, you agree not to engage in behavior contrary to these values at any Bioconductor-sponsored event (in person or virtual, including but not limited to talks, workshops, poster sessions, social activities), electronic communication channels (including but not limited to the Bioconductor Zulip space, the support site, online forums, the package review site, and social media communications), or packages (including commits). Furthermore, we require all participants to have identifiable accounts in Bioconductor online forums. Accounts that do not adhere to this after request to de-anonymise may be deleted.
We do not tolerate harassment, intimidation, or bullying of community members. Sexual language and imagery are not appropriate in presentations, communications or in online venues, including chats.
Any person violating the Code of Conduct may be sanctioned or expelled temporarily or permanently from an electronic platform or event at the discretion of the Code of Conduct committee.
The Bioconductor community is committed to ethical partnerships and avoiding partnerships with entities whose practices are inconsistent with Bioconductor values. We encourage community members to report or raise concerns about partnerships they deem unethical to the Code of Conduct committee via the reporting form.

title: Code of Conduct (U.S. English)
text:
sharing of ideas, code, software and expertise
collaboration
diversity and inclusivity
a kind and welcoming environment
community contributions



identity: gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, disability, physical appearance, ethnicity, body size, race, age, religion, language, etc.
intellectual position: approaches to data analysis, software preferences, coding style, scientific perspective, stage of career, etc.






Examples of unacceptable harassment, intimidation, and bullying behavior
Harassment includes, but is not limited to:

Making comments in chats, to an audience or personally, that belittle or demean another person
Sharing sexual images online
Harassing photography or recording
Sustained disruption of talks or other events
Unwelcome sexual attention
Advocating for, or encouraging, any of the above behavior

Intimidation and bullying include, but are not limited to:

Aggressive or browbeating behavior
Mocking or insulting another person’s intellect, work, perspective, or question/comment
Making reference to someone’s gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, disability, physical appearance, body size, race, age, religion, or other personal attributes in the context of a scientific discussion
Deliberately making someone feel unwelcome
Trolling behaviour (deliberately inflammatory or offensive messages)
Sustained off-topic posts

title: Code of Conduct (U.S. English)
text:
Enforcement
Anyone asked to stop harassing or intimidating behavior is expected to comply immediately.
If a person contravenes the Code of Conduct, the Code of Conduct committee retains the right to take any action that ensures a welcoming environment for all community members. This includes warning the alleged offender or temporary/permanent expulsion from the event and/or electronic platforms under Bioconductor’s control.
The Code of Conduct committee may take action to redress anything designed to, or with the clear impact of, disrupting an event or electronic communication platform or making the environment hostile for any community member.
We expect everyone in the Bioconductor community to comply with the Code of Conduct when participating in Bioconductor events and online communication platforms.

title: Code of Conduct (U.S. English)
text:
Reporting
If someone makes you or anyone else feel unsafe or unwelcome, please report it as soon as possible. You can make a report either anonymously or personally. All reports will be reviewed by the Code of Conduct Committee and will be kept confidential.

Electronically
You can make an anonymous or non-anonymous report via the following link: https://forms.gle/gEWHBWnXvZbEdFsq5. It is a free-form text box that will be forwarded to the Code of Conduct Committee. Alternatively you can email the Code of Conduct Committee (code-of-conduct@bioconductor.org). If you are uncomfortable reporting to the Code of Conduct committee as a group, you can contact any individual committee member via email or a direct message on the Bioconductor Zulip. Please include screenshots and/or copies of all relevant electronic conversations whenever possible (you don’t need to compromise your anonymity!).
We can’t follow up an anonymous report with you directly, but we will fully investigate it and take whatever action is necessary to prevent a recurrence.


Personal Report (for any Bioconductor events: in-person or virtual)
You can make a personal report to any member of the event Code of Conduct committee present at an event.
When taking a personal report, we will ensure you are safe and cannot be overheard. We may involve other event staff to ensure your report is managed properly. Once safe, we’ll ask you to tell us about what happened. This can be upsetting, but we’ll handle it as respectfully as possible, and you can bring someone to support you. You won’t be asked to confront anyone, and we won’t tell anyone who you are.
Our team will be happy to help you get the relevant support (e.g. help contacting hotel/venue security, local law enforcement, local support services, provide escorts, or otherwise assist you to feel safe for the duration of the event).
We value your attendance and participation at Bioconductor events and in our community.


Ombudsperson
We understand that you may want a person unrelated to Bioconductor overseeing your conflict resolution. To facilitate this, the Code of Conduct Committee will appoint an ombudsperson from a different open source community than members of the Bioconductor project. While they do not have power to establish, change or set aside decisions made by the Code of Conduct Committee, they can assist community members by offering consultation, mediation, coaching and referrals to other resources. The ombudsperson can be contacted directly via email (see below) to ensure a confidential, impartial, informal and independent process.


Incident procedure
The Code of Conduct Committee follows a standard procedure to deal with conflicts. This procedure is briefly summarized here. Incident procedures are based on the book “How to Respond to Code of Conduct Reports” by Valerie Aurora and Mary Gardiner.

title: Code de bonne conduite (Français, France métropolitaine)
text:
Version 1.2.0 (25 November 2022)
La communauté Bioconductor valorise une approche ouverte aux sciences favorisant:
Conformément à ces valeurs, Bioconductor se consacre à fournir une expérience accueillante, solidaire, collégiale, sans harcèlement, intimidation et intimidation, indépendamment de:
En participant à cette communauté, vous acceptez de ne pas adopter un comportement contraire à ces valeurs lors de tout événement parrainé par Bioconductor (en personne ou virtuel, y compris, mais sans s’y limiter, conférences, séminaires, presentations de posters, activités sociales), dans tout canal de communication électronique (y compris, mais sans s’y limiter, l’espace de travail Slack "community-bioc", le site de support, les forums en ligne, le site de revue de packages, et les communications sur les médias sociaux), ou dans tout package (y compris les commits). De plus, nous demandons à tous les participants de posséder des comptes identifiables sur les forums en ligne de Bioconductor.
Nous ne tolérons pas le harcèlement, l’intimidation ou la persécution des membres de la communauté. Le langage sexuel et l’imagerie sont inappropriés dans les présentations, les communications, ou les sites en ligne, y compris les discussions en ligne.
Toute personne qui enfreint le Code de conduite peut être sanctionnée ou expulsée temporairement ou définitivement d’une plate-forme électronique ou d’un événement à la discrétion du comité du code de conduite.

Exemples de harcèlement, d’intimidation et de comportements inacceptables
Le harcèlement inclut, mais ne se limite pas à :

Faire des commentaires dans les discussions en ligne, publiquement ou personnellement, qui déprécient ou dévalorisent une autre personne
Partager des images sexuelles en ligne
Harceler par le biais de photographie ou d’enregistrement
Interrompre de façon prolongée des présentations ou autres événements
Des avances sexuelle indésirables
Défendre ou encourager l’un des comportements ci-dessus

L’intimidation et la persécution incluent, mais ne sont pas limitées à:

Un comportement agressif ou intimidant
Se moquer ou insulter l’intelligence, le travail, la perspective, la question ou le commentaire d’une autre personne
Faire référence au sexe, à l’identité et à l’expression de genre, à l’orientation sexuelle, au handicap, à l’apparence physique, la taille, la race, l’âge, la religion ou d’autres attributs personnels dans le contexte d’une discussion scientifique
Délibérément faire quelqu’un se sentir rejeté
Un comportement de “trolling” (envoi de messages délibérément inflammatoires ou offensifs)
L’envoi continu de messages hors-sujet

title: Code de bonne conduite (Français, France métropolitaine)
text:
Mise en application
Toute personne invitée à cesser un comportement de harcèlement ou d’intimidation devrait se conformer immédiatement aux instructions reçues.
Si une personne contrevient au Code de conduite, le comité du Code de conduite se réserve le droit de prendre des mesures qui garantissent un environnement accueillant pour tous les membres de la communauté. Cela inclut l’avertissement du délinquant présumé ou son expulsion temporaire ou permanente de l’événement et/ou des plateformes électroniques sous le contrôle de Bioconductor.
Le comité du code de bonne conduite peut prendre des mesures pour réparer toute action visant à, ou causant clairement, la perturbation d’un événement ou d’une plateforme de communication électronique, ou rendant l’environnement hostile à tout membre de la communauté.
Nous demandons à tous les membres de la communauté Bioconductor de se conformer au Code de bonne conduite lorsqu’ils participent aux événements Bioconductor et aux plateformes de communication en ligne.
crumbs: Code de bonne conduite (Français, France métropolitaine)

title: Code de bonne conduite (Français, France métropolitaine)
text:
Signalement
Si quelqu’un vous fait sentir en danger ou indésirable, veuillez le signaler dès que possible. Vous pouvez remplir le formulaire de signalement de façon anonyme ou signé de votre nom. Tous les signalements seront examinés par le Comité du Code de bonne conduite et resteront confidentiels.

Electroniquement
Vous pouvez faire un rapport anonyme ou signé de votre nom via le lien suivant: https://forms.gle/gEWHBWnXvZbEdFsq5. Il s’agit d’une boîte de texte en forme libre qui sera transmise au comité du code de bonne conduite. Alternativement, vous pouvez envoyer un courriel au Comité du Code de bonne conduite (code-of-conduct@bioconductor.org). Si vous n’êtes pas confortable à l’idée de contacter l’ensemble du comité du code de conduite, vous pouvez contacter n’importe quel membre du comité par courriel ou un message direct sur l’espace de travail Slack “community-bioc”. Veuillez inclure des captures d’écran/copies de toutes les conversations électroniques pertinentes dans la mesure du possible (vous n’avez pas besoin de compromettre votre anonymat!).
Nous ne pouvons pas suivre un signalement anonyme directement avec vous, mais nous examinerons le signalement en profondeur et prendrons toutes les mesures nécessaires pour éviter une récidive.


Signalement direct (pour tout événement Bioconductor: en personne ou virtuel)
Vous pouvez faire un signalement directement à tout membre du comité du Code de bonne conduite présents à un événement.
Lorsque nous prenons un rapport direct, nous nous assurerons que vous êtes en sécurité et que personne d’autre ne peut épier la conversation. Il se peut que nous fassions appel à un autre personnel de l’évènement pour nous assurer que votre rapport est géré correctement. Une fois en sécurité, nous vous demanderons de nous faire part de ce qui s’est passé. Cela peut être bouleversant, mais nous traiterons toute information avec le plus grand respect possible, et vous pouvez vous accompagner de quelqu’un pour vous soutenir. On ne vous demandera pas de confronter qui que ce soit, et nous ne dirons à personne qui vous êtes.
Notre équipe se fera un devoir de vous aider à obtenir le soutien approprié (par exemple, aide à contacter la sécurité de l’hôtel/du lieu, les forces de l’ordre locales, les services de soutien locaux, escorte, ou tout support pour vous sentir en sécurité pendant la durée de l’événement).
Nous apprécions votre présence et votre participation aux événements Bioconductor et à notre communauté.


Médiation
Nous comprenons que vous voudrez peut-être voir la résolution de votre conflit gérée par une personne non liée à Bioconductor. Pour faciliter ceci, le comité du Code de bonne conduite nomme un médiateur (une médiatrice) associée à une autre communauté open source. Sans avoir la capacité d’établir, de changer, ou d’annuler les décisions prises par le comité du Code de bonne conduite, leur rôle leur permet d’aider les membres du comité par le biais de consultation, médiation, coaching, et références à d’autres ressources. Le médiateur (la médiatrice) peut être contacté(e) directement par email (voir ci-dessous) pour garantir un processus confidentiel, impartial, informel, et indépendent.


Procédure en cas d’incident
Le comité du Code de bonne conduite suit une procédure standardisée pour gérer les conflits. Cette procédure est brièvement résumée ici. Les procédures en cas d’incident sont basées sur le livre “How to Respond to Code of Conduct Reports”, co-écrit par Valerie Aurora et Mary Gardiner.

title: Contributing
text:
Proposing a change
Welcome, and thank you for your interest in contributing to the Bioconductor All-Community Handbook!
Everyone is welcome to help shape the Bioconductor All-Community Handbook. Whether you are new to Bioconductor or have been involved for years, your experience and perspective can help make this resource more useful and accessible. Contributions of all sizes are appreciated: fixing a typo, clarifying an explanation, sharing a resource, or suggesting a new topic. You do not need to be an expert in GitHub or write a finished chapter to get involved. Our ambition is to author this book as a community, drawing on our shared knowledge and diverse experiences.
The two main ways to contribute are to discuss ideas through GitHub issues and propose changes through pull requests.
Please follow our Code of Conduct in all interactions.
The handbook is maintained in a GitHub repository. Changes are proposed through pull requests, which let others read and discuss your edits before they become part of the handbook.

title: Contributing
text:
Fork the repository. A fork is your own copy of the repository on GitHub, where you can make changes freely.
Make your edits on a new branch. A branch keeps a set of related changes together. Edit the relevant files in your fork, either on GitHub or on your computer, and commit your changes with a short description.
Open a pull request. Propose merging your branch into the original repository’s main branch. Give the pull request a descriptive title and use the description field to briefly explain what you changed and why. If you would like early feedback, open a draft pull request and mention where you would like help.

title: Contributing
text:
Discussing contributions
You are welcome to open an issue directly on the book’s repository to discuss content you plan to add, suggest a change, flag a problem, or ask for help. For larger additions, sharing your ideas early can help you explore the scope and find others interested in contributing.
You can also reach out through the channels listed in Communicating with the community to gather ideas, ask questions, or find collaborators. You do not need a finished proposal to start a conversation.

title: Contributing
text:
Review and inclusion
Review is intended to be light-touch and collaborative. Contributions are reviewed for clarity, relevance, and consistency with the rest of the handbook. Clarifying questions may be asked and small edits may be requested. Feedback is a conversation: you are welcome to ask for clarification or help, and further commits to your branch will update the pull request automatically.
Once the contribution is ready and approved, a maintainer can merge it into the handbook.






TipAdditional resources



Contributing to The Turing Way links to useful resources on collaborating through GitHub and writing in Markdown, which can also help you contribute to this handbook.
